orderRules: "Day 1" through "Day 5" are lesson numbers, not weekdays. A family that starts on Tuesday or doubles up on Saturday is fine (§7), but the lessons go in order, one per day where possible, so the spacing does its work.

sections.title: 1. Purpose and place in the outline

blocks.text: The outline calls for rules-based spelling, not word lists (§3A). A child who knows why a word is spelled as it is can spell a thousand words they've never been drilled on. A child who memorized a list can spell the list. Each week of Grade 3 teaches one spelling rule, practices it in words and sentences, and checks it.

Vocabulary in Grade 3 is gathered, not imported: a few words a week from what the child is already reading in Literature and History, learned well enough to use. Latin and Greek roots begin in Grade 4 (§3A). Grade 3 prepares the ground with common prefixes and suffixes in Term 5, and Latin I (09) supplies the first roots informally.
Spelling sits in the daily core (§7) because spelling decays without frequent contact, and short daily practice beats one long weekly session.
The same pattern every week, so the child always knows what today is.

blocks.text: "Day 1" through "Day 5" are lesson numbers, not weekdays. A family that starts on Tuesday or doubles up on Saturday is fine (§7), but the lessons go in order, one per day where possible, so the spacing does its work.
36 weeks in 6 six-week terms.
5 short lessons a week, so 30 per term. Each lesson takes 5–8 minutes. The outline budgets 5 minutes a day for spelling in the daily core; vocabulary days run a little longer.
Everything is written in cursive (Penmanship, 04).

Each rule is taught when another course needs it. In particular, Grammar & Composition (02) defers to Spelling for the plural rules in its Term 2 week 11, and for -ly adverbs in week 9. Those rules come here first.

head: Term
Weeks
Rules
rows: Short vowels and closed syllables; -ck / -k; -tch / -ch and -dge / -ge; silent e (vowel–consonant–e); soft c and g; review week
Plurals with -s and -es; consonant + y to -ies; the -ly suffix and y to i (happily); irregular plurals (mice, geese, oxen); possessives with 's and s'; review week
Adding suffixes: the doubling rule (hop, hopping); dropping silent e (make, making); -ed and its three sounds; -ing; contractions; review week
Vowel teams (ai/ay, ee/ea, oa/ow); r-controlled vowels (ar, or, er/ir/ur); homophones (there/their/they're, to/too/two); review week
Prefixes un-, re-, dis-, pre-; suffixes -ful, -less, -ness; compound words; dividing words into syllables; review week
ie / ei; silent letters (kn, wr, mb); commonly confused words from the year's compositions; year-end review and dictation

blocks.text: Timing with Grammar:
Spelling Term 2 week 9 (-ly and y to i) matches Grammar Term 2 week 9 (adverbs).
Plurals come in weeks 7, 8 and 10, before Grammar's week 11 lesson on plural nouns. Grammar follows Spelling's wording.
Possessives come in week 11, the week before Grammar's week 12 lesson on possessive nouns.
Contractions in Term 3 come as Grammar teaches helping verbs (was not, wasn't).
Week 6 of every term is a review week: no new rule. The five lessons cycle back through the term's rules and end with a cumulative dictation.
Two words a week, chosen from that week's Literature or History reading: words the child met and might not know, such as apprentice, almanac, delegate, compromise, expedition, frontier.
Each term manual names the words in advance; a family may swap one for a word their child actually stumbled on.

Day 3 routine: say the word; read it in the sentence where the child met it; give a plain definition; the child says it back and uses it in a new sentence aloud. Then the word goes into the Memory Work queue (11) for a week of review.
Vocabulary words also appear in the Day 4 sentences and in the review slots of later checks.
No definitions to copy out. The aim is that the child uses the word, not that they write its dictionary meaning.
Term 5 prefixes and suffixes are where vocabulary and spelling meet: un- + happy, care + -less. That's the bridge to Grade 4's Latin and Greek roots.
Spelling owns the spelling in every course's compositions (Literature and Grammar & Composition both circle errors and leave scoring to Spelling).
When a parent circles a misspelled word in any written work, the correct spelling goes onto the child's personal list, a single page kept with the spelling notebook.
Up to three personal-list words join each Day 5 check. A word leaves the list after it's spelled correctly in two checks in a row.
If the word follows a rule already taught, the child says the rule while correcting it. That's the real test of whether the rule took.
Day 5 check: 10 words. 8 of 10 is mastery for the week.

Below 8: the missed words go onto the personal list. Below 6: the rule is not yet learned. Repeat that week's Day 1–2 lessons in the next week's slot and push the new rule back a week (§8: a missed concept is real, not a scheduling event). Use the review week to catch up.
Review week check (week 6 of each term): a cumulative dictation of 20 words from all the term's rules plus 2 sentences. 16 of 20 is the term standard; record it.
Year-end dictation (week 36): 30 words across all the year's rules plus a short passage. This is the Grade 3 exit check for spelling.
No spelling scores on compositions in any course. Spelling is scored only here.
Vocabulary is not tested in writing. The parent notes whether the child uses the word naturally, in narration or conversation, within the month.

blocks.text: Spelling is cumulative, but each lesson is short. If a family misses a few days, pick up at the next lesson, not the calendar day. Do not double the lessons to catch up: two lessons in one day undo the spacing that makes the daily core work.
A missed full week moves the sequence one week later; the term's review week absorbs it.

sections.title: 9. What each term manual will contain

blocks.text: For each week: the rule stated in a child's words, 10–14 example words (including a few exceptions, named as exceptions), the Day 2 build list, the two vocabulary words with the sentence they come from, the Day 4 sentences, and the Day 5 check list with its review words. For each term: a review-week plan and the cumulative dictation with its answer list.

glance.text: How to use each week.

Day 1, Rule: read the rule aloud; the child says it back. Read the example words; the child sorts them aloud by the rule. Point out the exceptions as exceptions: words that break the rule and simply have to be known.
Day 2, Build: dictate the build list. The child writes each word in cursive and says the rule aloud for any word they hesitate on.
Day 3, Vocabulary: say each word, give the context sentence, give the meaning, then have the child use it in a new sentence aloud. Add both words to Memory Work.
Day 4, Sentences: dictate both sentences. Each is read twice, then once more for checking.
Day 5, Check: dictate the 10 check words, plus up to three words from the personal list. Score out of 10, not counting the personal-list words.

Starting the personal list. In week 1, start a single page titled "My Words" at the back of the spelling notebook. From now on, words circled in Literature and Grammar & Composition go there (Plan §5).

blocks.text: Rule (say it back): "When a syllable ends with a consonant, it is closed, and its vowel usually says its short sound."
Examples: cat · step · fish · frog · hunt · plant · crust · list · camp · blend · trust · swim. Two-syllable: rab·bit, pic·nic, nap·kin: both syllables closed, both vowels short.
plant · step · crust · list · camp · frog · blend · swim · picnic · napkin

settler: a person who comes to live in a new place and build a home there. "The settlers built their fort beside the river." · colony: a settlement ruled by a faraway country. "Jamestown was the first lasting English colony."
"The settlers had to plant crops in the spring." · "Pocahontas could swim in the cold river."
trust · blend · hunt · swim · frog · plant · picnic · napkin · review: colony · settler
Rule: "At the end of a one-syllable word, use -ck right after a short vowel. Use -k after a consonant, a long vowel or two vowels."
Examples: -ck: back · deck · stick · clock · duck · black · truck · quick. -k: bank · milk · desk · ask · cook · speak · lake. Why lake? The a is long (silent e, week 4).
back · stick · clock · duck · black · bank · milk · desk · cook · speak

wilderness: wild land where no one has built farms or towns. "Sarah and her father walked for days through the wilderness." · courage: being brave when you are afraid. "Sarah had to keep up her courage in the dark forest."
"Sarah heard a stick crack in the black woods." · "She put on her cloak and kept up her courage."
stick · black · truck · quick · bank · milk · desk · speak · review: plant · trust
Rule: "Right after a short vowel, use -tch to spell /ch/ and -dge to spell /j/. After a consonant or any other vowel sound, use -ch and -ge."
Examples: -tch: catch · fetch · pitch · match · clutch. -ch: lunch · bench · porch · coach. -dge: badge · edge · bridge · lodge. -ge: huge · page · change · large.
Exceptions: much · such · rich · which (short vowel, but only -ch).
catch · fetch · match · lunch · bench · badge · edge · bridge · huge · large
pilgrim: a person who travels a long way for a holy reason. "The Pilgrims left England so they could worship God in their own way." · worship: to honor and pray to God.
"The Pilgrims crossed a bridge to reach the church." · "They had to change their homes much more than once."
catch · match · bench · porch · edge · bridge · large · which · review: clock · courage
Rule: "A silent e at the end of a word makes the vowel before it say its name."
Pairs to read aloud: cap/cape · kit/kite · hop/hope · cub/cube · pet/Pete. Then: make · ride · home · mule · these · flame · stone · while · shine · smoke.
Exceptions: have · give · live · come · some · done (the e is there, but the vowel doesn't say its name).
make · ride · home · stone · while · shine · smoke · flame · these · mule
voyage: a long trip by sea. "The Mayflower's voyage took more than two months." · compact: a written agreement. "The men signed the Mayflower Compact before they left the ship."
"The ship rode the waves for a long time on the voyage." · "Some of the men came on deck to see the stone shore."
stone · while · shine · smoke · flame · these · give · come · review: bridge · huge
Rule: "C says /s/ and g says /j/ when e, i or y comes next. Otherwise they say their hard sounds."
Examples: soft c: cent · city · cycle · ice · face · fence. Soft g: gem · giant · gym · page · cage. Hard: cat · cot · cup · gas · go · gum.
Exceptions (hard g before e or i): get · give · girl · gift.
city · face · ice · fence · giant · page · cage · gem · cup · gift

native: born in a place, or belonging there from long ago. "Squanto was a native of the land the Pilgrims settled." · fertile: able to grow good crops. "Squanto showed them how to make the soil fertile with fish."
"Squanto came to help the settlers at a giant feast." · "They put a fence around the fertile field."
city · ice · fence · giant · cage · page · girl · gift · review: home · catch

intro.text: No new rule. The five lessons cycle through the term.
Cumulative dictation (week 6, Day 5)
Words: plant · swim · napkin · crust · black · truck · milk · speak · catch · bench · edge · large · much · stone · shine · give · city · face · giant · girl.
Sentences: "The settlers came on a long voyage." · "Squanto gave them fish to make the field fertile."
Standard: 16 of 20 words. Words missed go onto the personal list. A rule with three or more misses gets one extra Day 1–2 pair at the start of Term 2, before week 7's new rule. Record the score.

blocks.text: The child says all five rules back. Sort a mixed pile of example words aloud: which rule does each follow?
Mixed: frog · quick · fetch · lodge · hope · cycle · napkin · desk · coach · giant

All ten words: settler, colony, wilderness, courage, pilgrim, worship, voyage, compact, native, fertile. The child uses each in a sentence aloud; any that come slowly stay in Memory Work for another week.
"The native people shared their fertile land." · "A brave pilgrim made the voyage to a new colony."
20 words and 2 sentences, below
Keep it short. Five to eight minutes. If the child is done in four, stop.
Say the rule, don't just correct. When a word is wrong, ask "Which rule is this?" before giving the answer.
Exceptions are not failures of the rule. Teach them as a small list of words that are "outlaws". Children enjoy knowing the outlaws.
Start the "My Words" personal list page in week 1
Add each week's rule and vocabulary words to the Memory Work queue
Record each Day 5 score, and the week 6 cumulative score

glance.text: Timed to Grammar & Composition. Grammar teaches adverbs in week 9, plural nouns in week 11 and possessive nouns in week 12, and follows this course's rules and wording. So the plural rules (weeks 7, 8 and 10), -ly (week 9) and possessives (week 11) all come here first.

Carry-over from Term 1. If a Term 1 rule had three or more misses in the week 6 dictation, spend the first two lessons of week 7 on it (Day 1–2 again), then teach week 7's rule over Days 3–5, with the vocabulary words moving to week 8's Day 3.
The daily pattern is the same as in Term 1 (see the Term 1 manual, "How to use each week").

blocks.text: Rule (say it back): "To make most nouns plural, add -s. If the word ends in s, x, z, ch or sh, add -es."
Why: you can hear the extra syllable. Box becomes box·es.
Examples: cats · kites · ships · boxes · buses · wishes · churches · foxes · glasses · buzzes · dishes · benches.
ships · kites · boxes · buses · wishes · churches · foxes · glasses · dishes · benches
apprentice: a young person who learns a trade by working for a master. "Ben was an apprentice in his brother's print shop." · trade: a kind of work that takes skill, like printing or candle-making.
"Ben made candles and soaps in his father's shop." · "The apprentice packed boxes of papers for the churches."
ships · boxes · wishes · churches · foxes · glasses · dishes · benches · review: giant · catch
Rule: "If a word ends in a consonant + y, change the y to i and add -es. If it ends in a vowel + y, just add -s."
Examples: consonant + y: city/cities · berry/berries · colony/colonies · pony/ponies · story/stories · penny/pennies. Vowel + y: day/days · boy/boys · key/keys · monkey/monkeys · valley/valleys.
cities · berries · colonies · stories · pennies · days · boys · keys · monkeys · valleys
thrift: using money and goods carefully, without waste. "Poor Richard's sayings teach thrift: 'A penny saved is a penny earned.'" · almanac: a yearly book of weather, dates and useful sayings.
"Ben saved his pennies and read many stories." · "The almanac told the farmers about the days ahead."
cities · colonies · stories · pennies · ponies · days · keys · valleys · review: buses · wishes
Rule: "To make an adverb, add -ly to the word: slow, slowly. If the word ends in a consonant + y, change the y to i first: happy, happily."
This is the same y-to-i change as week 8, now before a suffix. Grammar & Composition uses it this week for adverbs.
Examples: slowly · quickly · gladly · sadly · brightly · softly · happily · easily · busily · angrily · luckily · noisily.
Watch: shy, shyly and dry, dryly keep the y. These are rare; just note them.
slowly · quickly · softly · brightly · gladly · happily · easily · busily · angrily · luckily

invention: something new that someone makes for the first time. "The Franklin stove was one of Ben's inventions." · public: open to everyone, or belonging to the whole town. "Ben helped start a public library."
"Ben worked busily on his new invention." · "People happily borrowed books from the public library."
quickly · softly · brightly · happily · easily · busily · angrily · luckily · review: cities · keys
Rule: "Some nouns don't add -s at all. They change inside, or stay the same. These must be learned one by one."
Examples:
Change inside: man/men · woman/women · child/children · mouse/mice · goose/geese · tooth/teeth · foot/feet · ox/oxen · person/people.
Same both ways: sheep · deer · fish.
-f to -ves: leaf/leaves · wolf/wolves · loaf/loaves · knife/knives · half/halves.
men · children · mice · geese · teeth · feet · oxen · people · wolves · loaves
experiment: a test to find out whether an idea is true. "Ben flew a kite in a storm as an experiment." · electricity: a kind of power that makes lightning and sparks.
"The children watched Ben fly his kite in the storm." · "Two oxen pulled the cart, and the geese ran beside it."
women · children · mice · geese · feet · oxen · people · loaves · review: gladly · colonies
Rule: "To show that something belongs to one person or thing, add 's. To a plural that ends in s, add only '. To a plural that doesn't end in s, add 's."

Examples: one: Ben's kite · the dog's bone · the printer's shop. Plural ending in s: the colonies' laws · the farmers' market · the boys' coats. Plural without s: the children's books · the men's hats · the mice's hole.
Plural or possessive? the boys (more than one boy) · the boy's coat (one boy owns it) · the boys' coats (several boys own them).
(phrases) Ben's kite · the dog's bone · the printer's shop · the boys' coats · the farmers' market · the colonies' laws · the children's books · the men's hats · the mice's hole · the oxen's cart
ambassador: a person sent to speak for their country in another land. "Ben was America's ambassador to France." · treaty: a written agreement between countries.
"Ben's work in France helped the colonies' cause." · "The children's grandfather told them about the treaty."
(phrases) Ben's kite · the dog's bone · the boys' coats · the farmers' market · the colonies' laws · the children's books · the men's hats · the mice's hole · review: geese · busily

Plurals and possessives get confused. The apostrophe is the most common error in adult writing. Spend the time here and the payoff lasts a lifetime.

Irregular plurals come from Old English. If the child asks why it's mice and not mouses, the honest answer is that English is very old and kept a few of its oldest habits. It's a good story, not a flaw.
Personal-list words from Grammar's fable retellings start arriving in volume this term. Up to three join each check; no more.

glance.text: The term's idea: adding suffixes. Four of the five rules answer one question: what happens to a word when you add an ending? Sometimes you just add it (jump, jumping), sometimes you double (hop, hopping), sometimes you drop an e (hope, hoping). By week 16 the child should be able to decide which, for any word.

Timed to Grammar & Composition. Grammar teaches helping verbs in week 14 (was riding, had waited), which is full of -ed and -ing words. Contractions in week 17 come as the child is writing dialogue in Grammar's expand exercise, where contractions appear naturally ("I'll", "don't").

Carry-over from Term 2. If a Term 2 rule had three or more misses in the week 12 dictation, spend the first two lessons of week 13 on it, then teach week 13's rule over Days 3–5, with the vocabulary words moving to week 14's Day 3.
The daily pattern is the same as in Term 1 (see the Term 1 manual, "How to use each week").

blocks.text: Rule (say it back): "If a word has one syllable, one vowel, and ends in one consonant, double the last letter before adding an ending that starts with a vowel."
Call it the 1-1-1 rule. Count on three fingers.
Examples (doubles): hop/hopping/hopped · run/running · sit/sitting · stop/stopped · plan/planned · drum/drummer · big/bigger · swim/swimmer · shop/shopping.
Doesn't double:
jump, jumping: ends in two consonants
rain, raining: has two vowels
help, helpful: the ending starts with a consonant
Never double x or w: box, boxing; snow, snowing
hopping · running · sitting · stopped · planned · bigger · swimmer · jumping · raining · boxing
surveyor: a person who measures land and makes maps of it. "Young George worked as a surveyor in the Virginia wilderness." · frontier: the edge of settled land, where the wilderness begins.
"George stopped often to measure the land on the frontier." · "The surveyor was planning a long trip."
hopping · running · stopped · planned · bigger · shopping · jumping · boxing · review: children · happily
Rule: "Drop the silent e before an ending that starts with a vowel. Keep it before an ending that starts with a consonant."
Examples:
Drop: make/making · hope/hoped · ride/rider · brave/bravest · smile/smiling · write/writing · shine/shiny · use/using
Keep: hope/hopeful · care/careful · love/lovely · safe/safely · use/useless
The two rules together: hoping (from hope, drop e) and hopping (from hop, double). Say both aloud. The double letter keeps the vowel short.
making · hoped · rider · bravest · smiling · writing · using · hopeful · careful · safely
tax: money people must pay to their government. "The colonists were angry about the tax on tea." · rebel: a person who fights against the people in power.
"The rebels were writing letters against the tax." · "The bravest colonists were hoping for freedom."
making · hoping · hopping · writing · smiling · bravest · careful · lovely · review: sitting · swimmer
Rule: "-ed makes a verb past tense. It can sound like /t/, /d/ or /ed/, but it's always spelled -ed."
Examples by sound:
/t/: jumped · walked · kissed · wished · helped
/d/: filled · rained · played · called · rowed
/ed/, after t or d: wanted · planted · landed · needed · shouted
The sound changes; the spelling doesn't. Children who spell by sound write jumpt and landid. This rule fixes both.
jumped · walked · wished · filled · rained · played · wanted · planted · landed · shouted

patriot: a person who loves their country and works for it. "Paul Revere was a patriot who rode to warn the colonists." · militia: ordinary citizens who train to fight when needed. "The minutemen were part of the militia."
"Revere rowed across the river and landed safely." · "The militia waited and watched as the soldiers marched."
walked · wished · called · rowed · wanted · landed · needed · shouted · review: careful · riding
Rule: "To add -ing: just add it, double, or drop the e. And a final y always stays, because English never writes ii."
The decision, in order:
1. Does the word end in silent e? Drop the e: ride, riding.
2. Is it a 1-1-1 word? Double: run, running.
3. Does it end in y? Keep the y: cry, crying; carry, carrying.
4. Otherwise, just add: march, marching.
Examples: riding · coming · running · stopping · crying · carrying · hurrying · marching · reading · waiting.
riding · coming · running · stopping · crying · carrying · hurrying · marching · reading · waiting

retreat: to move back, away from danger or an enemy. "Washington's army had to retreat many times." · endure: to keep going through something hard. "The soldiers had to endure the winter at Valley Forge."
"The soldiers were marching and carrying heavy packs." · "They kept hurrying through the snow."
riding · coming · getting · stopping · crying · carrying · marching · waiting · review: planted · rained
Rule: "A contraction joins two words into one. An apostrophe takes the place of the missing letters."
Examples: do not, don't · is not, isn't · was not, wasn't · were not, weren't · can not, can't · I am, I'm · it is, it's · they are, they're · we will, we'll · you have, you've · let us, let's.
Outlaw: will not, won't (the spelling changes completely).
Watch out: it's means "it is". Its with no apostrophe means "belonging to it": "The bird built its nest." This is the most common contraction mistake.
don't · isn't · wasn't · can't · won't · I'm · it's · they're · we'll · let's
surrender: to give up and stop fighting. "The British surrendered at Yorktown." · victory: winning a battle or a contest.
"We'll cross the river tonight, and they won't expect us." · "It's cold, but the army didn't give up."
don't · wasn't · weren't · won't · it's · they're · we'll · you've · review: hurrying · bravest

intro.text: Cumulative dictation (week 18, Day 5)
Words: running · stopped · planned · jumping · boxing · making · writing · careful · safely · walked · played · landed · shouted · coming · crying · carrying · don't · can't · won't · it's.
Sentences: "The militia wasn't ready, but they stood and waited." · "We're hoping the army will endure the hard winter."
Standard: 16 of 20 words. Words missed go onto the personal list. A rule with three or more misses gets one extra Day 1–2 pair at the start of Term 4. Record the score next to Terms 1–2.

blocks.text: The child says all five rules back. Then give a word and an ending (shop + ing, hope + ful, carry + ing, plant + ed); the child says which rule decides the spelling.
Mixed: shopping · hoped · hopped · useless · wished · needed · hurrying · taking · couldn't · its (as in "its nest")
All ten words: surveyor, frontier, tax, rebel, patriot, militia, retreat, endure, surrender, victory. The child uses each in a sentence aloud.
"The patriots didn't surrender, and they won the victory." · "Washington was planning a surprise while the enemy was sleeping."
20 words and 2 sentences, below
The 1-1-1 rule is worth over-learning. It governs thousands of words, and it comes back in every grade. If week 13 shows below 8, repeat it before moving on, per the plan's mastery rule.
Say the decision aloud. In week 16 the child should talk through the four steps for each word. By week 18 they should do it silently.
The it's/its confusion is worth catching in all written work from now on. When it shows up in a Literature or Grammar composition, it goes on the personal list.

head: Rules
Vowel team ai/ay · ee/ea · oa/ow · r-controlled vowels · homophones · review week
rows: Vocabulary
Two words a week from Literature Term 4 (John Hancock, the Constitution, Toliver's Secret)
Lessons
5 a week, 5–8 minutes each: Day 1 Rule · Day 2 Build · Day 3 Vocabulary · Day 4 Sentences · Day 5 Check
Mastery
8 of 10 on each Day 5 check; 16 of 20 on the week 24 cumulative dictation

glance.text: The term's idea: two letters, one sound. Terms 1–3 dealt with single vowels and with endings. Term 4 deals with vowel sounds spelled by two letters together. The hard part is that one sound often has two spellings (rain, ray), so the child learns where each spelling goes in a word.

Carry-over from Term 3. If a Term 3 rule had three or more misses in the week 18 dictation, spend the first two lessons of week 19 on it, then teach week 19's rule over Days 3–5, with the vocabulary words moving to week 20's Day 3.
The daily pattern is the same as in Term 1 (see the Term 1 manual, "How to use each week").

blocks.text: Rule (say it back): "Ai and ay both say long a. Use ai in the middle of a word and ay at the end."
Why: English words don't end in i, so the y stands in at the end. (Remember y to i in Term 2? This is its partner.)
Examples: ai: rain · paint · train · chain · sail · wait · faint · plain. ay: day · play · stay · tray · away · delay · pray · display.
Outlaws: said, again (spelled with ai but not said with long a).
rain · paint · chain · sail · wait · plain · stay · away · delay · display
declaration: an important public statement. "The Declaration of Independence told the world why the colonies were breaking from Britain." · independence: being free to govern yourself.
"Hancock did not delay; he signed in plain sight." · "The ship had to wait for the rain to stop before it could sail away."
paint · train · chain · faint · plain · stay · delay · display · review: won't · writing
Rule: "Ee and ea both say long e. There's no rule for which one, so learn the words in families."
Examples: ee: tree · street · sleep · sweet · keep · green · speech · agree. ea: eat · read · seat · speak · team · leave · peace · reason.
Watch: ea sometimes says short e: bread · head · weather · ready. And great (long a) is an outlaw.
street · sleep · speech · agree · seat · speak · leave · peace · bread · ready
delegate: a person chosen to speak and vote for others. "Each state sent delegates to Philadelphia." · convention: a large meeting where people come together to decide something.
"The delegates could not agree, so they had to keep talking." · "They met in secret and did not speak to the people in the street."
street · speech · agree · sweet · peace · reason · leave · weather · review: delay · chain
Rule: "Oa and ow can both say long o. Use oa in the middle of a word and ow at the end."
This is the same middle/end pattern as ai/ay. Point that out; the child can predict it.
Examples: oa: boat · coat · road · loaf · soap · coast · float · groan. ow: snow · grow · slow · below · window · follow · elbow · shadow.
Watch: ow also says /ow/ as in cow, town, crowd, how. Read both sounds aloud and sort them.
boat · coat · road · loaf · coast · snow · grow · below · window · follow
constitution: the written plan for how a country is governed. "The delegates wrote a new Constitution for the United States." · union: a joining together of many into one.
"Ellen carried the loaf along the cold road." · "Snow fell below her window as she walked slowly."
coat · loaf · soap · coast · float · snow · below · shadow · review: speech · agree
Rule: "When r comes after a vowel, it changes the vowel's sound. Ar says /ar/ as in car. Or says /or/ as in fork. And er, ir and ur all say /er/, so learn which words use which."
Examples: ar: farm · star · march · sharp · party. or: horse · storm · north · short · story. /er/: er: her · fern · serve · term · ir: bird · first · girl · shirt · ur: turn · burn · hurt · church.

Help for er/ir/ur: group them into families. "The girl in the first shirt saw a bird." "Don't turn and hurt yourself running to church." "Her fern will serve for the whole term." Children remember sentences better than lists.
march · sharp · party · storm · north · serve · first · shirt · turn · church

compromise: an agreement where each side gives up something it wants. "The Great Compromise gave both big and small states a fair share." · debate: a formal argument where each side gives its reasons.
"The first debate lasted until the storm came." · "Both sides gave up part of what they wanted in the compromise."
march · party · north · short · serve · first · shirt · church · review: window · coast
Rule: "Homophones sound the same but are spelled differently and mean different things. You choose the spelling by the meaning."
The sets to learn:
there (a place: over there) · their (belonging to them) · they're (they are)
to (toward) · too (also, or more than enough) · two (2)
your (belonging to you) · you're (you are)
hear (with your ear; hear has ear in it) · here (this place)
know · no; right · write; knew · new
The contraction test: if you can say "they are" or "you are" in its place, use the apostrophe spelling.
(write the right word in each sentence, read aloud by the parent) there · their · they're · to · too · two · your · you're · hear · here

loyalist: a colonist who stayed loyal to the British king. "Some of Ellen's neighbors were loyalists." · occupied: held and controlled by an enemy army. "New York was occupied by the British during the war."
"Their city was occupied, and they're afraid to go out there." · "Ellen had two errands, and they were too dangerous to do alone."
(each word in a dictated sentence) there · their · they're · to · too · two · your · you're · review: first · storm

intro.text: Cumulative dictation (week 24, Day 5)
Words: paint · chain · away · delay · street · agree · peace · bread · boat · loaf · snow · window · farm · north · first · church · there · their · they're · too.
Sentences: "The delegates had to agree to a compromise." · "Their boat sailed away from the snowy coast."
Standard: 16 of 20 words. Words missed go onto the personal list. A rule with three or more misses gets one extra Day 1–2 pair at the start of Term 5. Record the score next to Terms 1–3.

blocks.text: The child says all five rules back. Point out the pattern in ai/ay and oa/ow: middle and end. Sort a mixed pile of words by vowel sound.
Mixed: train · display · sweet · reason · float · follow · sharp · fern · burn · here
All ten words: declaration, independence, delegate, convention, constitution, union, compromise, debate, loyalist, occupied. The child uses each in a sentence aloud.
"The delegates agreed to the compromise, and their union grew strong." · "You're right: the Declaration came first."
20 words and 2 sentences, below
Homophones need sentences, not lists. A child can't show they know their from there by spelling it alone. Every homophone check is dictated in a sentence.
Er, ir and ur are the hardest set in the term. There's no rule, only families. Expect several to go on the personal list, and don't worry about it.
Literature's early paragraph (week 24) and Grammar's paragraph work this term mean more writing, and more personal-list words. Hold the cap at three per check.

head: Rules
Prefixes un- and re- · prefixes dis- and pre- · suffixes -ful, -less and -ness · compound words · dividing words into syllables · review week
rows: Vocabulary
Two words a week from Literature Term 5 (tall tales, Johnny Appleseed, Lewis and Clark)
Lessons
5 a week, 5–8 minutes each: Day 1 Rule · Day 2 Build · Day 3 Vocabulary · Day 4 Sentences · Day 5 Check
Mastery
8 of 10 on each Day 5 check; 16 of 20 on the week 30 cumulative dictation

glance.text: The term's idea: words are built from parts. This is where spelling and vocabulary meet (Plan §4). A prefix or suffix changes a word's meaning in a predictable way: un- means "not", -less means "without". A child who knows the parts can work out a new word's meaning and its spelling. It's the bridge to Grade 4's Latin and Greek roots.

Day 3 changes slightly this term. Alongside the two Literature words, the child builds two or three new words from the week's prefix or suffix and says what they mean. Un- + known = unknown, "not known".

Carry-over from Term 4. If a Term 4 rule had three or more misses in the week 24 dictation, spend the first two lessons of week 25 on it, then teach week 25's rule over Days 3–5, with the vocabulary words moving to week 26's Day 3.
The daily pattern is the same as in Term 1 (see the Term 1 manual, "How to use each week").

blocks.text: Rule (say it back): "A prefix goes at the front of a word and changes its meaning. Un- means not or the opposite of. Re- means again or back. Adding a prefix never changes the spelling of the word itself."
So: un- + necessary = unnecessary, with two n's because both are needed. Nothing is dropped.
Examples: un-: unhappy · unkind · unknown · unlock · unfair · untie · unnecessary. re-: retell · rebuild · return · replant · reread · repay · rewrite.
unhappy · unkind · unknown · unlock · unfair · retell · rebuild · return · replant · rewrite

legend: an old story about a real or made-up hero, often stretched as it's retold. "Davy Crockett became a legend while he was still alive." · exaggerate: to make something sound bigger than it really is. Build: un- + true · re- + tell
"Each storyteller would retell the legend and make it bigger." · "It seems unfair, but some tall tales are untrue."
unhappy · unknown · unlock · unnecessary · retell · return · replant · rewrite · review: their · church
Rule: "Dis- means not or the opposite of, like un-. Pre- means before. The base word's spelling doesn't change."
Watch: dis- + satisfied = dissatisfied (two s's). The same rule as unnecessary: nothing is dropped.
Examples: dis-: disagree · dislike · disobey · disappear · dishonest · disloyal. pre-: preview · prepay · preheat · prefix · pretest · preschool.
disagree · dislike · disobey · disappear · dishonest · preview · prepay · preheat · prefix · preschool
orchard: a field of fruit trees. "Johnny Appleseed planted apple orchards across the frontier." · pioneer: one of the first people to settle in a new place. Build: dis- + appear · pre- + plan
"The pioneers did not disagree about the apple trees." · "Johnny would disappear into the woods and return with seeds."
disagree · dislike · disobey · disappear · disloyal · preview · preheat · prefix · review: rebuild · unkind
Rule: "-ful means full of. -less means without. -ness turns a describing word into a thing. The suffix -ful has only one l. If the word ends in consonant + y, change the y to i first."
The y-to-i change is the same as Term 2's happily. It's the same rule again: say so.

Examples: -ful: helpful · careful · hopeful · thankful · plentiful (plenty). -less: helpless · careless · fearless · endless · penniless (penny). -ness: kindness · darkness · sadness · happiness (happy) · emptiness (empty).
helpful · careful · thankful · plentiful · careless · fearless · endless · kindness · darkness · happiness

expedition: a long journey made for a special purpose. "President Jefferson sent Lewis and Clark on an expedition to the Pacific." · journal: a daily written record. "The captains wrote in their journals every night." Build: fear + -less · hope + -ful
"The expedition was careful in the endless forest." · "The captains were thankful for every kindness."
careful · thankful · plentiful · careless · fearless · penniless · darkness · happiness · review: disappear · preview
Rule: "A compound word is two whole words joined to make a new one. Keep every letter of both words."
So: book + keeper = bookkeeper (two k's); room + mate = roommate. Nothing is dropped, just as with prefixes.
Examples: campfire · sunset · riverbank · snowshoe · horseback · moonlight · footprint · cornfield · nightfall · somewhere · bookkeeper.
Watch: some pairs stay as two words (ice cream, post office). When unsure, check a dictionary. That's a skill too.
campfire · sunset · riverbank · snowshoe · horseback · moonlight · footprint · cornfield · nightfall · somewhere

interpreter: a person who explains what someone is saying in another language. "Sacagawea served as an interpreter with the Shoshone." · territory: a large area of land. Build: river + bank · horse + back
"Sacagawea rode on horseback along the riverbank." · "At nightfall they lit a campfire in the moonlight."
campfire · riverbank · horseback · moonlight · footprint · nightfall · somewhere · bookkeeper · review: fearless · kindness
Rule: "Every syllable has one vowel sound. To spell a long word, say it slowly, clap the syllables, and spell one syllable at a time."
Dividing patterns to say back:
Between two consonants (VC/CV): rab·bit, win·ter, nap·kin. The first vowel is short.
Before a single consonant (V/CV): ti·ger, pa·per, mu·sic. The first vowel is long.
Keep prefixes and suffixes whole: re·turn, care·ful, dark·ness.
Examples: winter · basket · hundred · tiger · paper · music · Pacific · Missouri · mountain · traveler · expedition (ex·pe·di·tion).
(child claps, then writes) winter · basket · hundred · tiger · paper · music · mountain · traveler · Pacific · expedition

summit: the very top of a mountain. "From the summit they could see more mountains ahead." · continent: one of the earth's great land masses. "They crossed the continent to the Pacific Ocean." Build: clap con·ti·nent and sum·mit
"In the winter the travelers crossed the mountains." · "After a hundred days, they saw the Pacific."
winter · basket · hundred · tiger · mountain · traveler · Pacific · expedition · review: horseback · somewhere

intro.text: Cumulative dictation (week 30, Day 5)

Words: unknown · unnecessary · return · rewrite · disagree · disappear · preview · prefix · careful · plentiful · fearless · penniless · happiness · darkness · campfire · riverbank · bookkeeper · winter · mountain · traveler.
Sentences: "The fearless travelers did not disagree about the plan." · "At nightfall they wrote in their journals by the campfire."
Standard: 16 of 20 words. Words missed go onto the personal list. A rule with three or more misses gets one extra Day 1–2 pair at the start of Term 6. Record the score next to Terms 1–4.

blocks.text: The child says all five rules back. Then the parent gives a prefix or suffix and a base word, and the child builds and spells the new word and says its meaning: un + lucky, care + less, empty + ness, re + turn.
Mixed: unfair · rewrite · dishonest · prepay · hopeful · penniless · emptiness · snowshoe · roommate · music
All ten words: legend, exaggerate, orchard, pioneer, expedition, journal, interpreter, territory, summit, continent. The child uses each in a sentence aloud.
"The pioneers were thankful for the plentiful orchards." · "Their journals described the endless mountains of the territory."
20 words and 2 sentences, below

"Nothing is dropped" is the term's one big idea. Prefixes, compound words and most suffixes keep every letter. The only change is the y-to-i the child already knows. Children who double-check this rule stop writing unecessary and bookeeper.
Word-building is play. Let the child invent words: un- + banana? It's not a word, but they understand what it would mean. That understanding is the real goal.
Literature's tall tale (week 30) is a good place to see the new prefixes and suffixes used naturally. Words circled there go on the personal list as usual.

head: Rules
ie and ei · silent k, w and b · silent gh · commonly confused words · year review · year-end dictation
rows: Vocabulary
Two words a week from Literature Term 6 (Abraham Lincoln), weeks 31–35; week 36 reviews the year
Lessons
5 a week, 5–8 minutes each: Day 1 Rule · Day 2 Build · Day 3 Vocabulary · Day 4 Sentences · Day 5 Check
Mastery
8 of 10 on each Day 5 check; 24 of 30 on the year-end dictation, the Grade 3 spelling exit standard

glance.text: The term's shape. Three new rules (weeks 31–33), one week built from the child's own personal list (week 34), then two weeks of review: Terms 1–5 in week 35, and the year-end dictation in week 36.

Carry-over from Term 5. If a Term 5 rule had three or more misses in the week 30 dictation, spend the first two lessons of week 31 on it, then teach week 31's rule over Days 3–5, with the vocabulary words moving to week 32's Day 3.
The daily pattern is the same as in Term 1 (see the Term 1 manual, "How to use each week").

blocks.text: Rule (say it back): "I before e, except after c, or when it sounds like a, as in neighbor and weigh."
Examples: ie: piece · field · chief · believe · niece · shield · fierce. After c: receive · ceiling · receipt · deceive. Sounds like a: neighbor · weigh · eight · sleigh · vein.
Outlaws: their, weird, seize, either. The rhyme covers most words; the outlaws must be learned.
piece · field · chief · believe · shield · receive · ceiling · neighbor · weigh · eight

humble: plain and simple; not proud or showy. "Abe was born in a humble log cabin in Kentucky." · chore: a small job that has to be done regularly. "Young Abe's chores included chopping wood and carrying water."
"Abe's family worked in the field near their humble cabin." · "Their neighbor gave them a piece of bread and eight apples."
piece · field · believe · fierce · receive · ceiling · neighbor · eight · review: careful · disappear
Rule: "Some letters are written but not said. K is silent before n (kn). W is silent before r (wr). B is silent after m (mb)."
Why: long ago, English speakers said these letters. The sounds dropped away; the spellings stayed.
Examples: kn: know · knee · knife · knock · knot · knew · knowledge. wr: write · wrong · wrap · wrist · wreck · wrote. mb: lamb · climb · thumb · comb · crumb · limb.
know · knife · knock · knowledge · write · wrong · wrist · wrote · climb · thumb
ambition: a strong wish to do something important. "Abe had a great ambition to learn." · scholar: a person who studies and learns a great deal.
"Abe wrote his sums on a wooden board by the fire." · "He would climb into the loft to read, and he knew many books by heart."
knife · knock · knowledge · write · wrong · wrote · climb · thumb · review: believe · weigh
Rule: "Gh is often silent. After i, it makes i say its name (igh). In -ought and -aught, it says nothing at all."
Examples: igh: light · night · right · fight · bright · high · sigh. -ought: thought · bought · brought · fought · ought. -aught: taught · caught · daughter · naughty.
Outlaws: laugh, enough, rough, tough: here gh says /f/. Learn them as their own small family.
light · night · bright · high · thought · brought · fought · taught · caught · enough

flatboat: a large boat with a flat bottom, used to carry goods down a river. "As a young man, Abe helped take a flatboat down the Mississippi to New Orleans." · cargo: the goods a boat or wagon carries. "The flatboat's cargo was corn, pork and flour."
"The flatboat carried its cargo all the way to New Orleans." · "He had brought the flatboat down the river and caught sight of the city lights."
night · bright · high · thought · brought · fought · taught · daughter · review: knowledge · climb

weeks.title: Commonly confused words (from the child's own list)

blocks.text: Rule: "Some words are easy to mix up because they look or sound alike. You choose by the meaning."
This week is built partly from the child's own personal list. Before Day 1, look through it: which confusions keep coming back?
The core set (use these if the personal list doesn't supply enough):
then (next, at that time) · than (comparing: taller than)
were (past of are) · where (a place) · we're (we are)
are · our (belonging to us)
its (belonging to it) · it's (it is), from Term 3
lose (to not have any more) · loose (not tight)
a lot (always two words)
(each word in a dictated sentence) then · than · were · where · we're · are · our · its · lose · loose

integrity: being honest and doing right even when no one is watching. "Abe walked miles to return a few pennies; he was a man of integrity." · lawyer: a person trained in the law who helps people in court.
"We're going to the store where Abe worked." · "He was more honest than anyone, and our town knew it."
(each word in a dictated sentence) then · than · were · where · we're · our · loose · a lot · (plus up to three personal-list words) · review: thought · taught

intro.text: No new rule. Each lesson reviews part of the year; the child says the rules back and spells a few words from each.

blocks.text: Short vowels, -ck, -tch/-dge, silent e, soft c/g; plurals, -ies, -ly, irregular plurals, possessives. Say each rule; spell two words for each.
The 1-1-1 rule, dropping e, -ed, -ing, contractions; vowel teams, r-controlled vowels, homophones. Same routine.

candidate: a person who is trying to be chosen for a job, such as president. emancipation: setting people free. "The Emancipation Proclamation declared freedom for enslaved people in the rebelling states."
Prefixes, suffixes, compound words, syllables; ie/ei, silent letters, confused words. Same routine.
A short practice run of 15 words drawn from all six terms. Not recorded; it's to warm up for week 36.

intro.text: Year-end dictation (week 36, Days 3–4)
Part 1 (Terms 1–3): napkin · truck · bridge · stone · giant · boxes · cities · happily · children · the boys' coats · hopping · making · landed · carrying · won't.
Part 2 (Terms 4–6): display · speech · window · church · their · unnecessary · disagree · thankful · riverbank · mountain · believe · neighbor · knowledge · thought · than.

Passage (Day 4, after Part 2): "Abe Lincoln grew up in a humble cabin. He was hungry for knowledge, and he read every book he could find. Later he became a lawyer, and then the president. People knew him as a man of integrity."

Standard: 24 of 30 words. This is the Grade 3 spelling exit standard. The passage isn't scored by the word; note any rule the child clearly hasn't absorbed. Words missed start the child's Grade 4 personal list. A child below 24 begins Grade 4 with a short review of the rules they missed, before Latin and Greek roots begin.
